course_description:
The scale and scope of automation is an increasingly persistent feature of our everyday lives. In this course, students will engage with the deeper context of our faith in algorithms, and the aspirations, anxieties, ambitions and fantasies that have brought them to life. Course content will explore the science, ethics, politics and sensory experience of automation, from its historical inception to its technocratic and popular applications in contemporary life and the spaces we inhabit. Students will develop a grounded knowledge of the value systems shaping automated systems in the modern world, before progressing to a critical evaluation of the automated future that is central to the ambitions of contemporary digital cultures.

In this course, you will examine and engage with the aspirations, anxieties, ambitions and fantasies that have characterised our understanding of, and experiences with, automation. You will explore the science, ethics, politics and sensory experience of automation, from its historical inception to its technocratic and popular applications in contemporary life, focusing especially on the rise ofﾠ algorithmic culture and artificial intelligence. This course provides a grounded knowledge of the value systems shaping automated systems in the modern world, before progressing to a critical evaluation of the automated future that is central to the ambitions of contemporary digital cultures.

assessment_details.task_description: Overview This assessment is completed in class during 8 of your tutorials, in total. It is designed to help you reflect on your understanding of key concepts from the readings and tutorial activities, improve your ability to apply those concepts, and enhance your participation in tutorials. You will complete structured entries in a learning journal each week during the listed weeks. Learning journal entries will be handwritten in class and collected by your tutor for assessment each week. We will reserve 15 minutes for completion of journal entries at the end of tutorials. A total of 8 opportunities are provided to complete learning journal entries across the semester, each worth 6%. Only your best 5 results will be counted, together forming 30% of your final grade. The assessment builds in the flexibility to miss up to 3 sessions with no penalty and no documentation required. There are no opportunities to re-take an individual learning journal entry, and no alternative assessment is available except in the specific circumstances set out below. This is a device-free assessment classified as “Secure” under UQ’s rules for using AI in assessment : “This assessment is designed to protect academic integrity and assess your understanding of course concepts. You must only use the approved materials and tools for this assessment task. Use of prohibited materials in this task may be investigated and treated as academic misconduct.” Use of AI, electronic devices and any form of pre-prepared written or other materials are not permitted for this assessment . Journal entries can only be completed in class. Alternative assessment and accommodations If you have a Disability Action Plan relevant to this task, please contact the course coordinator as early as possible. Reasonable accommodations can be made for matters documented in a Disability Action Plan (for example, if you are unable to handwrite under timed conditions). A detailed marking rubric and complete task description can be found in your Assessment 1 folder. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.task_description: Overview This assignment has two components: a digital poster design, and a peer engagement coordination. During your first tutorial, you will be allocated a week in which to present your digital poster and coordinate peer engagement. You will submit your digital poster via the Turnitin link on Blackboard. The submission link is in your Assessment 2 folder. For this assignment, you will be assessed on the content and quality of your digital poster and the quality of your peer engagement coordination . The rubric and complete task description is available in your Assessment 2 folder. During the Week 1 tutorial, you will be allocated a week in which to present your digital poster and facilitate discussion. Length: 5-minute Digital Poster Presentation + 5-minute Peer Engagement Coordination Recording of Oral and Practical Assessment All presentations will be recorded for marking purposes via recording facilities available where the assessment takes place (eg. ECHO360, Zoom, camera device) Recordings will be retained by the School of Communication and Arts for at least 12 months from the release of the final grade for the course. Recordings will be stored in a secure manner and will only be accessed by authorised school staff for the purposes of: Moderation of marking; Provision of feedback to the student(s) recorded; and/or Re-marking following a successful re-mark application. assessment_details.title: Ethnographic Fieldwork & Analytical Report
assessment_details.task_description: Word Count: 1,500 – 2,000 words (excluding references) Overview In this course, we explore how cultures shape, resist, and are reconfigured by automated systems. Rather than treating automation as an abstract phenomenon external to our lives, this assessment tasks you with acting as a participant-observer within your own classroom community. Throughout the semester, three students each week will deliver a poster presentation and coordinate peer discussions during tutorials. Your task is to track, document, and analyse these live, unrecorded exchanges. You will select two specific tutorial sessions as your raw "field sites" and build a critical analytical report evaluating how the conceptual friction generated in those discussions reflects broader cultural concerns surrounding automated systems. The assignment rubric and complete task description is provided in the Assessment 3 folder on Blackboard. Read full task description Hide full task description

policies_and_procedures: University policies and procedures apply to all aspects of student life. As a UQ student, you must comply with University-wide and program-specific requirements, including the: Student Code of Conduct Policy Student Integrity and Misconduct Policy and Procedure Assessment Procedure Examinations Procedure Reasonable Adjustments for Students Policy and Procedure AI for Assessment Guide Recording of Teaching Policy and Procedure Learn more about UQ policies on my.UQ and the Policy and Procedure Library . Course guidelines Communication Expectations While you are a student at UQ, all communication must be conducted according to the UQ Student Code of Conduct . The UQ Library has a helpful Communicate and collaborate online module . Email is the primary way for you to send messages to, and receive information from, the School and our staff. You must use your UQ email address (not a private address) to communicate with staff. You should add a clear subject line, including course code, and a 2-3 word statement. You can send email at any time, however, please do not expect responses outside normal working hours (Monday to Friday from ~8am to ~5pm). Emails that constitute bullying, harassment or discrimination against staff contravene the Student Code of Conduct. Emails like this will be reported to the University, and the matter will be pursued as misconduct. Learning activities
